newsitem.title: USA: U.S. homes more affordable in Q4 - NAR.
newsitem.headline: U.S. homes more affordable in Q4 - NAR.

text.p: A drop in home prices and stable mortgage rates made U.S. homes more affordable in the fourth quarter of 1996, according to a survey by the National Association of Realtors issued Monday.
The real estate industry group's housing affordability index rose to 127.0 in the fourth quarter from 120.0 in the third quarter, but was down from 129.0 in the fourth quarter of 1995.

When the NAR index measures 100, a family earning the median income has exactly the amount needed to buy a single-family home at the median price, using conventional financing and a 20 percent down payment.

For the fourth quarter, the median home price was $117,600, the median family income was $40,922, and mortgage rates averaged 7.71 percent. In the third quarter, the median price was $120,500, median family income was $40,581 and the mortgages were an average 7.96 percent.
Qualifying income for conventional financing was $32,217 in the fourth quarter, down from $33,824 in the prior quarter.

The NAR said the first-time buyer index, which shows the ability of renters to qualify for a mortgage, also rose in the fourth quarter. That index rose to 80.7 from 76.3 in the third quarter, but was still below 82.0 in the fourth quarter 1995.

Despite the increase in home affordability for first-time buyers, the NAR said the gap between qualifying income and median income, about $6,000, is still a problem for those wanting to buy their first home.
"Still, many first-time buyers are struggling to overcome down payment and loan qualification problems," John Tuccillo, NAR's chief economist, said in a statement.
